raw_case_text: A 4-month-old infant presented with complaints of cough, cold, and breathlessness that had persisted for 2 days. The baby's oral intake had been very poor the earlier day. Initial clinical examination revealed bilateral wheeze on auscultation and subtle dysmorphic facial appearance which included small chin, small mouth, and coarse facial features. The mother gave history of uneventful postnatal period. The baby had received all the necessary vaccines required for her age. The mother also gave history of abortion of her previous pregnancy during the 2nd trimester because of cardiac anomaly identified on fetal ultrasound (USG) scan. In view of its difficulty in breathing, the baby was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and was started on oxygen and nebulization. Nasopharyngeal aspirate showed positivity for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bronchiolitis. Blood gas analysis showed respiratory acidosis. In view of respiratory distress and acidosis, the baby was intubated and started on synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation (SIMV) mode. Blood cultures were negative. Echocardiogram (ECHO) was done and found to be normal. Chest radiograph frontal projection showed bilateral air space opacities with right upper lobe consolidation suggestive of pneumonia [Figure 1]. The baby was started on antibiotics and oral Ribavirin. During the next day in ICU, the child had seizures. Biochemistry analysis showed reduced calcium level of 5.7 mg/dl (normal value: 8.5-10.1 mg/dl). 25-Hydroxy-vitamin D level was low and measured 13.4 ng/ml (normal value: <20 ng/ml). The parathyroid hormone (PTH) level was normal in spite of the low calcium. The baby was started on 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol and calcium. Blood investigations showed low hemoglobin measuring 7.5 g/dl (normal value: 11-14 g/dl) and a total WBC count of 10,700 cells/ml. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) blood analysis showed positivity for cytomegalovirus (CMV). Flow cytometery of lymphocytes showed combined T-cell and B-cell immunodeficiency. In spite of good antibiotic cover and physiotherapy, the right upper lobe consolidation was persistent. Intravenous immunoglobulin and steroids were started to treat persistent infection, following the hematologist's advice. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest with intravenous contrast showed hypoplastic thymus [Figure 2a] and right upper lobe consolidation [Figure 2b]. CT chest with maximum intensity projection (MIP) and volume-rendered (VR) images showed aberrant right subclavian artery [Figure 3a and b]. In view of dysmorphic facial features, chest infection, hypoplastic thymus, immunodeficiency, hypocalcemia, and decreased vitamin D, with a previous history of abortion of the fetus because of cardiac anomaly, a strong possibility of DGS was suspected. Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) study was done to look for chromosomal defects. The results showed deletion of chromosome 22q11.2 [Figure 4], which confirmed the diagnosis of this rare entity. The baby's respiratory distress gradually settled and the infant was discharged on the parent's request.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-month-old female infant presented with a 2-day history of cough, coryza, breathlessness, and poor oral intake.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy in the postnatal period and up to date on age-appropriate vaccinations, the infant developed 2 days of cough, cold, and progressive respiratory distress with poor feeding the day prior to admission, requiring ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and subsequent management of hypocalcemic seizures on ICU day 2.
subjective.past_medical_history: Uneventful postnatal history and age-appropriate immunizations. Maternal/family history: mother had a prior second-trimester therapeutic abortion due to a fetal cardiac anomaly detected on prenatal ultrasound.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2 days of cough, cold, breathlessness, poor oral intake, and ICU day 2 seizures.

objective.physical_examination: Respiratory distress with bilateral wheezing on chest auscultation and subtle dysmorphic facial features including micrognathia (small chin), microstomia (small mouth), and coarse facial features; developed generalized seizures on ICU day 2.
objective.routine_investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV); arterial blood gas showed respiratory acidosis; blood cultures negative. ICU day 2 biochemistry: severe hypocalcemia with serum calcium 5.7 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.1 mg/dL), low 25-hydroxyvitamin D at 13.4 ng/mL (normal >20 ng/mL), and inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone (PTH). CBC: hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL (normal 11-14 g/dL) and WBC 10,700 cells/uL. Chest radiograph showed bilateral airspace opacities with persistent right upper lobe consolidation; transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood PCR was positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV). Lymphocyte subset flow cytometry demonstrated combined T-cell and B-cell immunodeficiency. Contrast-enhanced chest CT with MIP and volume-rendered reconstructions revealed a hypoplastic thymus, right upper lobe consolidation, and an aberrant right subclavian artery. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) confirmed a chromosome 22q11.2 deletion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of DiGeorge syndrome (chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome; confirmed by FISH 22q11.2 deletion, thymic hypoplasia, aberrant right subclavian artery, combined T- and B-cell immunodeficiency, and hypoparathyroid hypocalcemia) presenting with RSV bronchiolitis and cytomegalovirus (CMV) co-infection/pneumonia (confirmed by positive blood CMV PCR and persistent right upper lobe consolidation). Managed with SIMV mechanical ventilation, antibiotics, oral ribavirin, calcium and 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol) supplementation, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and systemic corticosteroids, with gradual resolution of respiratory distress and discharge upon parental request.
